summary: DMARC lets a domain owner state policies for message validation and reporting, but the basic capability does not let a Public Suffix Domain (PSD) set a policy for names below it. This experimental document extends DMARC to give PSDs that capability. It was replaced by RFC 9989.

eli5.summary: Big shared domains like country-level endings have not been able to set mail safety rules for the sites below them. This experiment gives them that power. It was replaced by RFC 9989.

subtitle: Extending DMARC policy to top-level and multi-part domains

tldr.problem: DMARC (RFC 7489) lets domain owners set email safety policies, but only at the organizational level. Public Suffix Domains like .gov or .co.uk cannot set policies for subdomains below them, allowing impersonation of non-existent addresses.
tldr.mechanism: This experimental extension lets Public Suffix Operators (PSOs) publish DMARC records at the PSD level and adds a new 'np' tag for non-existent subdomains. Mail receivers check PSD DMARC records as a fallback when a domain has no policy of its own.
tldr.outcome: This was an experimental test of PSD DMARC functionality that was replaced by RFC 9989, which standardized changes to DMARC handling of public suffixes.

today: RFC 9091 was an Experimental extension to DMARC that was replaced by RFC 9989 in September 2024, which standardized PSD DMARC functionality and made permanent changes to how DMARC handles public suffix domains.

sections.title: The DMARC Gap for Shared Domains
sections.content:
DMARC (RFC 7489) lets a domain owner publish a policy that mail receivers should apply to messages claiming to come from their domain and its subdomains. However, DMARC treats Public Suffix Domains (PSDs) like .gov, .bank, or .co.uk differently: it does not let a PSD owner publish a policy that applies to names registered under the PSD unless a specific DMARC record exists for each registrant.

This creates a security gap. An attacker can send mail from a non-existent domain like phishing.gov.example, and a mail receiver will not find a DMARC policy to apply, because no one has registered "phishing.gov.example" and published a DMARC record for it. The receiver must guess what to do. This experimental RFC lets PSOs publish a policy that covers non-existent subdomains.
sections.eli5: Normally, DMARC lets a company post rules about its own mail. But shared domains like .gov belong to many companies. Attackers can send fake mail from non-existent company names under .gov because no one owns them. This experiment says a .gov operator can post rules that apply to the whole .gov domain.

sections.title: Terminology and Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC introduces key definitions: a Public Suffix Domain (PSD) is a point in the DNS tree where independent organizations can register names, like .com or .gov.uk. An Organizational Domain is a name registered under a PSD, such as example.com. The Longest PSD is the parent PSD of an Organizational Domain (for example.com.co.uk, the longest PSD is .co.uk).

Two types of PSOs would benefit: branded PSDs like .google (which are effectively single-organization domains listed in the public suffix list for DMARC purposes), and multi-organization PSDs like .bank that require DMARC deployment. For multi-organization PSDs, PSD DMARC applies to non-existent domains, allowing organizations that do not publish DMARC to inherit the PSD's policy.
sections.eli5: A Public Suffix is a place where you can register domains: .com, .gov, .co.uk. An Organizational Domain is what you register: example.com. The Longest PSD is the biggest shared piece: .co.uk in example.com.co.uk.

sections.title: The New DMARC Tag and Policy Discovery
sections.content:
The extension adds a new DMARC tag, np (non-existent subdomain policy). When a PSO publishes a DMARC record at the PSD level with an np tag, it specifies how mail receivers should handle messages from non-existent subdomains. The syntax is identical to the standard DMARC p tag: none, quarantine, or reject.

When a mail receiver checks a message from a domain like phishing.gov.example, it first looks for a DMARC record at that exact domain. If none exists and the Longest PSD is listed in a registry of DMARC PSDs, the receiver queries for a DMARC record at the PSD (gov.example). The np tag (or the fallback p tag) is applied to non-existent domains. Importantly, if an Organizational Domain publishes its own DMARC record, the PSD policy is not used.
sections.eli5: Receivers check for mail rules in order: first at the company (example.gov), then at the shared domain (.gov). A new 'np' tag tells what to do about non-existent companies.

sections.title: Deployment and Data Leakage Risks
sections.content:
Implementations using PSD DMARC query a registry to determine which PSDs are participating. The RFC provides samples at psddmarc.org, available as a DNS query service, an IANA-like registry, or formatted like the public suffix list for easy integration.

The primary concern is privacy. When mail receivers send DMARC Aggregate Reports (RUA) to PSOs about messages from non-existent domains, they reveal information about attack patterns and infrastructure. For single-organization PSDs like .google, this is acceptable since the PSO controls all domains. For multi-organization PSDs like .bank, feedback about non-existent domains carries little privacy risk. However, for PSDs like .com that do not mandate DMARC, any non-DMARC organization could have its feedback redirected to the PSO, which is privacy-sensitive. To mitigate this, PSD DMARC Feedback must be limited to Aggregate Reports only (never detailed Forensic Reports), and multi-organization PSDs must limit feedback to non-existent domains unless they mandate DMARC.
sections.eli5: Mail systems report problems back to the domain owner. With .gov doing it, the .gov operator learns about attacks on every .gov address, even ones that do not exist. That is useful, but it can also leak private information about which companies are being targeted.

sections.title: Security and DNS Risks
sections.content:
PSD DMARC amplifies the security risks documented in RFC 7489. DNS cache poisoning or name chaining attacks have wider scope because compromising a PSD-level DMARC record affects all subdomains, not just one organization. The RFC also notes that the risk of External Reporting Addresses being abused (sending reports to attacker-controlled systems) is amplified: by design, PSD DMARC sends unrequested reporting to entities external to the Organizational Domain.

A clarification is made to address an existing DMARC interoperability issue: some implementations incorrectly bypass DMARC processing for domains listed in public suffix lists. This RFC clarifies that domain names on a public suffix list are not exempt from DMARC policy application and reporting.
sections.eli5: If someone hacks the DNS records for .gov, they affect all .gov sites at once, not just one. And sending reports to the .gov operator means the .gov operator learns about attacks.
